w: On 9 May 2001, a stampede inside this stadium killed 126 people -- the worst stadium disaster in Africa's history, and the second-deadliest in the sport's history anywhere. The ground still stands and still hosts football; the tragedy is part of what any visit here now carries.
s: Africa's deadliest stadium disaster, 126 dead in one night.
_facts: stampede at Ohene Djan Stadium in Accra, 9 May 2001
killed 126 people, worst stadium disaster in Africa's history
second-deadliest disaster in football history behind the Estadio Nacional disaster

w: Everything from land snails to car parts changes hands in this market at the heart of Accra -- a sprawl of stalls run overwhelmingly by women traders. Handcrafted bead jewellery sits beside school stationery and secondhand clothes; if it's sold in the city, odds are it passes through here first.
s: Land snails to car parts -- Accra's market has it all.
_facts: market place and shopping district in the center of Accra
sells everything from car parts to land snails, fresh produce, clothes, tools, medicines
dominated by women traders
jewellery from locally handcrafted beads also sold

w: Standing 28 metres over Jamestown, this lighthouse has guided ships into Accra's harbor since the early 1930s, built to replace an 1871 original that had done the job for sixty years before it. It shares its patch of coast with Fort James right next door.
_facts: lighthouse in the Jamestown district of Accra, approximately 28 metres tall
constructed early 1930s to replace an earlier 1871 structure
key navigational aid for vessels entering the port of Accra
stands next to Fort James

w: Ghana's national mosque since 2021 holds 15,000 worshippers, making it the second-largest in West Africa -- and the whole ten-million-dollar complex, imam's residence, madrasa and library included, was a gift from Turkey's Hudai Foundation, backed by the Turkish government.
s: West Africa's second-largest mosque -- a gift from Turkey.
_facts: national mosque of Ghana since 2021
capacity for 15,000 worshippers, second-largest mosque in West Africa
built at a cost of US$10 million, funded by the Turkish Hudai Foundation with support of the Turkish government
complex includes imam's residence, madrasa and library
located at Kanda (Kawukudi)

w: This arch anchors Black Star Square, the monument complex Ghana built to mark its 1957 break from British colonial rule. Alongside the Black Star Gate and the Liberation Day Monument, it turns one plaza into a running timeline of the independence struggle.
s: The arch at the heart of Ghana's independence square.
_facts: national monument at Black Star Square (Independence Square), Accra
part of a complex commemorating independence from British colonial rule in 1957
forms a complex with the Black Star Gate and the Liberation Day Monument

w: Ghana's first Latter-day Saint temple was built from Makore wood and Namibian pearl granite, chosen to echo local materials rather than import a foreign look. More than 17,000 people filed through the public open house before its 2004 dedication by church president Gordon B. Hinckley.
s: Ghana's first LDS temple, built from local stone and wood.
_facts: first Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints temple in Ghana
single-story structure using local materials, Makore wood and Namibia Pearl granite
public open house drew more than 17,000 visitors
dedicated by Gordon B. Hinckley on 11 January 2004

w: Founded in 1975 by Swami Ghanananda Saraswati, this Odorkor complex is widely considered the first Hindu monastery established and led by indigenous Africans. It has since become the anchor of Hinduism among ethnic Ghanaians, with branches spreading across the country and into neighboring Togo.
s: Africa's first Hindu monastery, led by Africans.
_facts: Hindu monastic and temple complex headquartered in Odorkor, a suburb of Accra
founded 1975 by Swami Ghanananda Saraswati
widely regarded as the first Hindu monastery established and led by indigenous Africans
branches across Ghana and in Togo

n: George Padmore Research Library on African Affairs
w: Kwame Nkrumah built this Osu library in 1961 as a memorial to Pan-Africanist writer George Padmore, stocking it with archives of anti-racist and anti-colonial movements -- pamphlets, campaign papers, journals from the 1960s-90s. By law, it's Ghana's only library required to hold a copy of every book published.
s: A 1961 library built to archive Pan-African struggle.
_facts: public library in Osu, Accra, built by Dr Kwame Nkrumah in memory of George Padmore
built 30 June 1961
claimed to be the only library/research center in Ghana mandated by law to receive a legal deposit
collections include archives of cultural, educational, political and anti-racist campaign groups from the 1960s-1990s

w: This monument honors Gold Coast veterans of Burma's WWII campaign who marched peacefully on Christiansborg Castle after coming home -- and were fired on for it. Seven were killed; the shooting became one of the sparks that lit the road to Ghanaian independence.
s: Where WWII veterans marched home and were shot for it.
_facts: monument in Accra honoring veterans of the Burma campaign of WWII
veterans marched peacefully towards Christiansborg Castle after returning to the Gold Coast
protesters were fired upon; seven veterans were killed

w: Ghana's oldest museum opened in 1957, the same year as independence, and has been collecting ever since -- more than 10,000 objects of archaeology, ethnography and fine art. A 2015 closure for restoration kept it shut for seven years; it reopened in 2022, library and conservation lab intact.
s: Ghana's oldest museum, seven years in restoration.
_facts: established 1957, the largest and oldest of six museums under the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board
closed 2015 for restoration, reopened 2022
approximately 10,000 or more objects: archaeology, ethnography and fine art
includes a library, conservation laboratory and education hall

w: Ghana's first president is buried here, at the center of a downtown park built in his honor -- one of the country's ten most-visited sites, drawing roughly 98,000 people a year. Kwame Nkrumah rests beside his wife Fathia, beneath a mausoleum designed specifically to be the park's centerpiece.
s: Where Ghana's founding president lies, still drawing crowds.
_facts: Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park and Mausoleum, downtown Accra
approximately 98,000 visitors annually, one of the top 10 most visited sites in Ghana
mausoleum houses the remains of first president Kwame Nkrumah and his wife Fathia Nkrumah

w: Built in 1673 as a gold-and-slave trading post for the Royal African Company, this fort joined Dutch and Danish strongholds already dotting the Gold Coast. It later did colonial time as a prison -- one that held Kwame Nkrumah himself in 1950-51, years before he became the president honored a few kilometers away.
s: A slave-trade fort that later jailed a future president.
_facts: fort built by the Royal African Company of England in 1673 as a trading post for gold and slaves
joined Dutch Fort Crèvecoeur (1649) and Danish Fort Christiansborg (1652) on the Gold Coast
UNESCO World Heritage List, 1979
served as a prison from the colonial era to 2008
Kwame Nkrumah was imprisoned there 1950-1951
